articles.summary: Hayden Panettiere’s estranged mother and former manager, Lesley Vogel, has spoken out about her daughter’s shocking death at the age of 36. In an interview with NBC News, Vogel said, “I think Hayden was an amazingly talented person in so many departments and I think young people who grow up in the…
body: When the memoir was released, Vogel told Page Six that she believed “the present drama is partially to sell books…As many parents of entertainment children [know], we are all too familiar with the painful observation of watching the self-destructive paths they sometimes choose. No parent hopes for this scenario; we want our children to be the best of themselves and live a peaceful, joyful life. Sadly, this is out of our control. You cannot save someone who does not want to be saved.”

Regarding her mother, Panettiere told Us Weekly that “unfortunately, we don’t have a relationship right now” but “that doesn’t mean that I don’t leave the door open for the opportunity to present itself one day.” Vogel added in her NBC News interview, “I just feel that she’s with her brother and they’re at peace.” Panettiere’s younger brother Jansen died at 28 in 2023.

articles.title: Frank Beard, Longtime ZZ Top Drummer, Dies at 77
articles.summary: Frank Beard, ZZ Top’s longtime drummer for the past 56 years, has died. He was 77. A representative for Beard confirmed that he died while in hospice care at his ranch in Richmond, Texas, with his family by his side.
body: Frank Beard, ZZ Top ‘s longtime drummer for the past 56 years, has died. He was 77.
The band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2004. The band’s co-founder, bassist Dusty Hill, died in 2021.

While ZZ Top was best known for their synthesizer-powered 1980s hits, they were a thoroughly Texan, heavy rock-blues band at heart, spawned from the same psychedelic scene that birthed Roky Erickson and the 13th Floor Elevators but keeping things roots and rocking throughout their more than 50-year career, even as they incorporated synthesized rhythms into their sound in the 1980s.

Though not a founding member of ZZ Top, Beard had played with the group since their debut “First Album” in 1971 through their most recent studio effort, 2012’s “La Futura,” as well as two recent live albums. Although Gibbons and Hill were renowned for their flowing beards, Beard sported only a mustache; Gibbons famously said, “Frank’s beard is on his driver’s license.”

articles.title: How the ‘Hacks’ Production Team Created a ’70s Sitcom Set and Overcame Las Vegas-Sized Challenges
articles.summary: In the “Hacks” universe, “Who’s Making Dinner?” is a fictional sitcom celebrating its 50th anniversary at PaleyFest with a screening and party. The story goes that the sitcom was created in the 1970s by Deborah (Jean Smart) alongside her late husband, Frank.
body: Tokarz drew from tones for the living room and décor from “All in the Family,” landing on a color palette of avocado shades, oranges and creams. “We wanted to live in that space with the wood paneling because it’s such a tip to that era. While we did pull out tones from ‘All in the Family,’ we wanted to uplift the actual architecture,” he explains. “And of course, when it comes to sitcoms, the couch is so incredibly important — it’s the focal point of just about everything we’ve ever seen.”

Jennifer Lukeheart, the show’s set decorator, searched far and wide. Ultimately, she found the seating in a surprising location: Facebook Marketplace. “It had the texture and tones that we were working with, and it had all the beats,” says Tokarz. The couch wasn’t all that paid homage to the past — the pass-through and doors used on “Hacks” were assets taken from the archives of TV history from the “Will and Grace” set, specifically from the episodes where the show honored “I Love Lucy.”
As part of the PaleyFest sequence, Tokarz and his team took a few pieces from the set dressing and built that out.

articles.title: Phyllida Law, prolific performer across stage and screen, dies aged 94
articles.summary: As adept at comedy and musicals as she was drama, Law also acted alongside daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson in a career spanning eight decades. Phyllida Law, whose prolific acting career encompassed a wide range of stage, TV and film roles – a number of which were alongside her daughters, Emma…
body: Born in Glasgow in 1932, Law was accepted at the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theatre school – initially intending to be a stage designer but then switching to acting. She appeared in a number of Bristol Old Vic productions in the 1950s, and it was there she met Eric Thompson, a fellow actor, whom she married in 1957.

From the late 80s she achieved more prominence in film, appearing alongside daughter Emma in Peter’s Friends (directed by Thompson’s then husband Kenneth Branagh), Much Ado About Nothing (again with Thompson and Branagh), and the Gwyneth Paltrow-led adaptation of Jane Austen’s Emma alongside her other daughter Sophie. Law then appeared with Emma – playing mother and daughter – in The Winter Guest, Alan Rickman’s feature film directing debut, which won considerable acclaim.

Law continued to appear in high-prestige TV shows, including Waking the Dead, Rosemary & Thyme, Foyle’s War, Doc Martin and Agatha Christie’s Poirot, and had a recurring role in the Stephen Fry lawyer comedy drama Kingdom as Fry’s Aunt Auriel. Her final screen role was in the 2020 romance Then Came You, written by and starring Kathie Lee Gifford.
points: As adept at comedy and musicals as she was drama, Law also acted alongside daughters Sophie and Emma Thompson in a career spanning eight decades.

articles.title: Match review – gory and slyly satirical catfishing horror for the age of Hinge
articles.summary: Online dating’s eternal bugbear reaches a horrific apotheosis in this funny, grimy and impishly directed shocker. Paola (Humberly González) is a pretty young woman about to turn 30 who hasn’t found herself a steady boyfriend – so, like many people of her generation, she’s on all the dating apps.
body: Of course, Paola should have listened to her sister. The good looking guy (played by Luke Volker) turns out to have been a catfishing lure, and the real Henry (Jacques Adriaanse) looks like what you’d get if a troll mated with a slime mould. Plus, it’s actually Henry’s deranged mother, Lucille (a fantastic Dianne Simpson) who’s been writing all those courtly messages to Paola – who is soon sedated with drugged wine and wakes up about to be raped, exactly the sort of scenario your actual mother warned you about.

Fortunately, it’s not all grim worst-nightmare-ever stuff, thanks to a slyly witty script credited to Al Kaplan and Jon Kaplan, directed with impish verve by Danishka Esterhazy. There are some very funny scenes, including a great two-hander between Lucille and another possible victim, Natalie (Nikita Faber), who hasn’t been completely honest about her own presentation online. The last stretch has lashings of practical effect gore to keep the genre fans happy, but it’s the sour social satire that lingers in the imagination afterwards.

articles.summary: With the Empire speaking Welsh in a new release, the Cardiff-born actor's force awakens as Han Solo.
body: Hollywood star Matthew Rhys has revealed he was "too scared" to talk to Harrison Ford about being the voice of Han Solo in a new Welsh language adaptation of Star Wars.
The experience of taking on the iconic role was "weird", added the 51-year-old from Cardiff, who moved to the US to pursue a career in acting.
Star Wars will be dubbed in Welsh for the first time ahead of the sci-fi classic's 50th anniversary next year, and has been praised by the First Minister.
But the Welsh Conservatives called a £100,000 contribution from the Welsh government "out of touch" when thousands of NHS patients wait for treatment.

articles.title: ‘There was a certain hostility’: how Wet Hot American Summer went from miss to hit
articles.summary: Critics might have been sniffy back in 2001 but the silly summer camp comedy has endured and director David Wain has been enjoying the ‘slow-burn’ appreciation. In the summer of 2001, the film critic Roger Ebert wrote a scathing film review in song form, with lyrics set to the tune of a classic…
body: Twenty-five years later, the film’s director and co-writer, David Wain, joined several of its stars on the vast lawn of the Autry Museum in Los Angeles to sing the review to a crowd of thousands, many of them wearing Camp Firewood T-shirts and 80s-style sweat absorbers. The performance preceded an anniversary screening of what has become a cult classic.

Ebert was one of many critics at the time who seemed baffled by the comedy, which follows the absurd adventures of a group of horny and/or lovelorn counselors desperate to make the most of their final day of camp in 1981. But if those early critics didn’t quite get it, plenty of viewers later did – enough to warrant two Netflix series, a place on various lists of the best films of the century, and a return to theaters this month to mark its 25th anniversary.
points: Critics might have been sniffy back in 2001 but the silly summer camp comedy has endured and director David Wain has been enjoying the ‘slow-burn’ appreciation.

articles.title: Waves Turn review – the exhausting, joyful, boring, wondrous realities of new motherhood
articles.summary: Josephine Ahnelt’s gentle but truthful documentary has home-movie intimacy and some incredibly touching moments. As a piece of art depicting motherhood, Judith Rohrmoser’s self-portrait of breastfeeding sticks two fingers up at the tradition of the Madonna with child.
body: Rohrmoser is one of five women who agreed to be filmed at their most vulnerable in the first year of motherhood for this Austrian documentary. It’s a gentle but truthful look at new motherhood, making the point that – ignore the Renaissance artists – having a tiny baby does not put you in perpetual state of bliss. The reality is exhaustion, joy, boredom, wonder and a rush of other feelings. Director Josephine Ahnelt shoots in 16mm, her camera up close, filming with the intimacy of a home video, cutting off heads to at one point zero in on what interests her: a mother snipping her baby’s tiny fingernails.

The women share their experiences in voiceover. One mother says she didn’t experience the all-encompassing love she was told she’d feel when her baby was placed on her chest; instead, it happened little by little. Another talks about the judgmental comments she gets about bottle feeding her baby after struggling to breastfeed. One woman says she didn’t believe friends that her relationship would be changed by having a baby. Now she knows.
points: Josephine Ahnelt’s gentle but truthful documentary has home-movie intimacy and some incredibly touching moments.

articles.title: Actress Phyllida Law, mother of Emma and Sophie Thompson, dies at 94
articles.summary: Law appeared in films alongside both of her daughters, Dame Emma and Sophie, including 1996's Emma.
body: Stage and screen star Phyllida Law, the mother of fellow actresses Dame Emma and Sophie Thompson, has died at the age of 94.

"It is with great sadness we have to announce that Phyllida Law died supremely peacefully at home, surrounded by all of her family, on Monday 27th July," her manager Jacky Leggo said in a statement to BBC News.
"We had worked together for over fifty years and she was a beautiful person inside and out."

Law appeared on screen alongside her daughters several times throughout a long and varied career, including in the 1996 adaptation of Jane Austen's Emma, starring Gwyneth Paltrow. Law played Mrs Bates while Sophie played her daughter Miss Bates.

articles.title: ‘Nashville’ Alum Charles Esten Notes “Strange Coincidence” of Being in Greenville, South Carolina Days Before Hayden Panettiere’s Death
articles.summary: The actor says he "wish[es]" he'd had a chance to see and reconnect with Panettiere as he recalls how they became "fast friends" during the audition process and early days of making ABC drama series.
body: Nashville alum Charles Esten is among those remembering late actress Hayden Panettiere after she died unexpectedly Sunday at the age of 36.
Esten, who played Deacon Claybourne on the ABC drama, also lamented a missed opportunity to reconnect with his former co-star before she died.
He and wife Patty Hanson were in Greenville, South Carolina, where Panettiere died on Sunday, on Friday night while he was on tour.

He added, “Such a strange coincidence. I just wish that it had actually put us there together at the same time. And that we somehow could have bumped into her. And got to hug her, and laugh in amazement with her.”
